note.question: How do competition, regulation, and uncertainty—A global game approach interact?
note.overview: When a government agency considers tightening a standard on a pollutant, the agency often takes into account the proportion of firms that are able to meet the new standard (what we refer to as the industry’s “voluntary adoption level”) because a higher proportion indicates a more feasible standard. The paper develops a novel model of regulation in which the probability of a stricter standard being enacted increases with an industry’s voluntary adoption level. To analyze such strategic interaction among firms’ decisions under correlated and uncertain payoffs, we use the global game framework recently developed in economics.

When a government agency considers tightening a standard on a pollutant, the agency often takes into account the proportion of firms that are able to meet the new standard (what we refer to as the industry’s “voluntary adoption level”) because a higher proportion indicates a more feasible standard.
For example, there were about 40 car brands in the United States in 2008 (Marks 2008), and the EPA considered 108 gasoline reﬁneries when proposing the Tier 3 Gasoline Sulfur Standard (EPA 2014a).
To analyze such strategic interaction among firms’ decisions under correlated and uncertain payoffs, we use the global game framework recently developed in economics.

conditions: There exists a threshold b(2) (> 2ε) such that, if the competition intensity b ≤b(2), there exists a purestrategy equilibrium.
In this equilibrium, firm i (∈[0, 1)) adopts the green technology if and only if xi ≥x(2), where x(2) b/2+fL −fH +(1−q)(fH −mL) r/(r+1).

The condition that b < (1 −q)( fH −mL) corresponds to the effect of government regulation being sufficiently strong such that if all other firms adopt the technology, firm i is encouraged to adopt the technology.

conditions: If x1 −2ε ≤ x(2) ≤x1 +2ε, then firm 1 expects that some firms observe signals higher than x(2), and the voluntary adoption level is positive.

In addition, a higher signal x1 affects the substitutability effect and the complementarity effect: With a higher fundamental θ, other firms’ signals xi for i ∈[0, 1) are more likely to be higher as well.

So if x1 + 2ε < x(2), firm 1 knows that no other firms observe signals higher than the threshold x(2), that is, the voluntary adoption level α is zero, and the marginal effect of a higher x1 on α is also zero.
